chunks: As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated, from Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-ʿAlawī, from al-ʿAmrakī, from ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar, from his brother Mūsā (peace be upon him):
He said: I asked him about a man who had a nosebleed and then blew his nose, so that the blood became small pieces and fell into his vessel. Is it permissible to perform wudu from it?
He said: If there is nothing visible in the water, there is no objection. But if there is something clearly apparent, then wudu shall not be performed from it.
The appropriate interpretation of this report is to understand it as follows: when that blood is like the head of a needle — imperceptible and undetectable — then such an amount is pardoned.

key_terms.يَسْتَبِينُ: becomes visible / discernible in the water

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on performing wudu with water that has small blood fragments from a nosebleed in it?
ai.summary: This hadith records ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar's question to Imam Mūsā al-Kāẓim (AS) about whether wudu remains valid when water is contaminated by small blood fragments expelled from a nosebleed. The Imam rules that if no blood is discernible in the water there is no objection, but if blood is clearly apparent then wudu is impermissible from it. Shaykh al-Ṭūsī appends a jurisprudential gloss interpreting the hadith to apply specifically to blood of needle-head size — below the threshold of sensory perception — which is legally excused.
